basics.title: Speak in the first person
basics.body: Say "I need your signature," not "She says she needs your signature." Speak as the person you are interpreting, and keep their pronouns. Use the third person only to clarify something as the interpreter ("The interpreter needs to clarify...").

basics.title: Don't add, omit, or change
basics.body: Convey everything that was said, including tone and hesitations. Do not soften bad news, summarize, or give advice. If you do not know a word, say so rather than guessing.

basics.title: Ask to repeat
basics.body: It is professional to ask for repetition or clarification. Say to the speaker: "The interpreter requests a repetition." Ask them to speak in short chunks of one or two sentences.

basics.title: Stay neutral and confidential
basics.body: Do not give your opinion, take sides, or discuss the meeting afterward. Introduce your role at the start and explain that everything is confidential.

basics.title: Use usted
basics.body: Address parents formally with usted unless they invite otherwise. Verbs: "puede", "tiene", "firme", "venga" (not "puedes", "tienes", "firma", "ven").

basics.title: Handle acronyms and jargon
basics.body: Expand acronyms the first time (IEP, ELL, 504). If a concept has no Spanish equivalent, explain it briefly and tell the speaker you did so.

basics.title: Seat and eye contact
basics.body: Sit slightly behind or beside the parent and speaker so they look at each other, not at you.

basics.title: Know your limits
basics.body: If a meeting involves legal, medical, or highly technical content beyond your level, tell the school and request a qualified interpreter.

basics.title: Gender of the child
basics.body: Use "hijo" for a son and "hija" for a daughter. If you do not know, use "su hijo o hija" or the child's name, and ask.
